avg_hr_scored.description: What the engine will actually DIVIDE BY when it scores this session: the in-band mean of its HR stream when one spans at least half the session, the stored `avg_hr` otherwise (#311). Publishing it here is what makes a broken reading detectable from the listing (#319). Before, `avg_hr` was echoed raw beside `hr_known: true` and an agent had to apply the 35-220 bound itself — which stopped identifying refused rows once the engine began scoring from streams, since a session can store 18 bpm and score perfectly well. The rule now: a row is refused by the EF and speed/HR lenses exactly when `avg_hr_scored` is outside 35-220, and the two fields disagreeing means the stored summary was computed from a lossy stream. `hr_known` still answers the separate question of whether a reading was recorded at all.

date_known.description: Whether `date` could be read. False means the row's stored `start_local` is NULL, empty, malformed, or dated before year 1000 — `date` is then an empty string, which is a HOLE and not a value. Needed because an empty date string already means something else in this contract: SKILL.md documents `last_hard_session_date` as `'' = none on record`, so without this flag a consumer cannot tell 'no such thing exists' from 'it exists and its date is unreadable'. #249 chose to REPORT these rows rather than refuse, because a listing cannot turn a wrong date into a wrong answer, and hoists them to the top so no limit hides them; this is the field that says which ones they are.

rankable.description: Whether the engine will give this row a ranking position. False means `start_local` is unusable as a timestamp — either its DATE half is unreadable (see `date_known`) or its TIME half is, as in `2026-08-23T37:00:00Z`, which has a perfectly readable date. These are the rows `stride activities` HOISTS to the top as needing repair, so this is the field that says why row one is row one. `rankable` means chronologically orderable: a row can be unrankable and still appear on a `top` leaderboard, carrying the same needs-repair meaning `date_known` does. It licenses no magnitude — unlike the `_known` flags, which each vouch for a value published beside them.
